The two sets ask different questions on purpose: the chapter exercises in [Appendix G](solutions.qmd) are reading-and-study material, while the worksheets are what participants fill in during a session. Each part below keeps the worksheet's code and condenses the written answers to the points that matter. ## Julia essentials for modelers — Day 1, Session 1 Worksheet: `worksheets/01-julia-essentials-for-modelers.qmd`. The chapter is [Julia essentials for modelers](../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd). ::: {#ws-p01-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using CairoMakie using StableRNGs check(name, condition) = println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint") println("Julia version: ", VERSION) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Julia version: 1.12.5 ``` ::: ::: ### Part A — writing a model kernel ::: {#cell-ws-p01-a1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} p = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0) u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0] # S, I, R function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t) S, I, R = u λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N # force of infection, λ = βcI/N du[1] = -λ * S # dS/dt du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I # dI/dt du[3] = p.γ * I # dR/dt return nothing end du = zeros(3) sir_ode!(du, u0, p, 0.0) check("dI/dt is 2.45 at the baseline", isapprox(du[2], 2.45; atol = 1e-9)) check("dR/dt is 2.50 at the baseline", isapprox(du[3], 2.50; atol = 1e-9)) check("nobody is created or destroyed", any(!iszero, du) && isapprox(sum(du), 0.0; atol = 1e-12)) du ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ dI/dt is 2.45 at the baseline ✓ dR/dt is 2.50 at the baseline ✓ nobody is created or destroyed ``` ::: ::: {#ws-p01-a1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: -4.95 2.45 2.5 ``` ::: ::: #### A1. Interpret - At the starting state $\lambda = 0.005$ per day, giving derivatives $(-4.95,\; 2.45,\; 2.50)$. They sum to zero: the 4.95 people per day leaving $S$ arrive in $I$, and 2.50 per day move on to $R$, so $I$ nets $4.95 - 2.50 = 2.45$. - The exact numbers carry the weight here, not the shape of the answer. Both rates are positive and a sum does not care about order, so the $I$ and $R$ lines written the wrong way round would pass a sign check and the conservation check alike. That is why every later unit validates against a number the theory fixes in advance. **Why `du[2] = ...` rather than `du = [...]`** - `du[2] = ...` writes into the array the caller already made, so the caller sees the change. `du = [...]` points the local name at a new array and leaves the caller's untouched, so the function appears to do nothing. - Experiment 1 shows it: `x` is still `[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]` after `build_new_array` and `[10.0, 2.0, 3.0]` after `write_into_array!`. Both return `nothing`, and both lines are legal Julia, so the difference never surfaces as an error. - A solver calls the kernel thousands of times; allocating a fresh three-element array each call leaves the garbage collector cleaning up work that never needed doing. **Where the answer went** - `return nothing` is literal. In experiment 2 `returned` is `nothing`, while `du_trial` has gone from three `NaN`s to `[-4.95, 2.45, 2.5]`. - Julia passes arguments by sharing, so the `du` inside the function and the `du` outside are two names for one array. The trailing `!` is the convention that marks an argument as being modified. **`p.β` versus `p[1]`** - Positional access encodes the *order* of the parameters into every line that uses them. In experiment 3, `p.β` gives `0.05` from both tuples, while `p[1]` gives `0.05` from one and `1000.0`, the population size, from the other. - Nothing errors, and every answer downstream is wrong. `p.β` either finds the field or raises an error immediately, which is the difference between a silent failure and a loud one. ### Part B — the same calculation over a whole grid ::: {#ws-p01-b1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt) # numerically stable 1 - exp(-r δt) δts = 0.0:0.25:10.0 γ = 0.25 # the session's recovery rate, per day linear = γ .* δts # the shortcut, elementwise — note the dot on the `*` probs = rate_to_proportion.(γ, δts) check("one value of each for every δt", length(probs) == length(δts) && length(linear) == length(δts)) check("every probability stays between 0 and 1", !isempty(probs) && all(0 .<= probs .<= 1)) check("the shortcut escapes [0, 1]", !isempty(linear) && maximum(linear) > 1) check("the two agree when δt is small", length(probs) > 1 && length(linear) > 1 && isapprox(probs[2], linear[2]; rtol = 0.05)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ one value of each for every δt ✓ every probability stays between 0 and 1 ✓ the shortcut escapes [0, 1] ✓ the two agree when δt is small ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ws-p01-rate .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (720, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "window width δt (days)", ylabel = "probability") hlines!(ax, [1.0]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "probability = 1") lines!(ax, δts, linear; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "shortcut γ δt") lines!(ax, δts, probs; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 3, label = "1 - exp(-γ δt)") axislegend(ax; position = :rb) ylims!(ax, 0, 2.6) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ws-p01-rate .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Probability of at least one event in a window of width δt at rate γ = 0.25, against the linear shortcut γ δt. ::: ::: #### B1. Interpret - The two are nearly indistinguishable while $\gamma\,\delta t$ is small: $0.0606$ against $0.0625$ at $\delta t = 0.25$ (3% high), $0.221$ against $0.250$ at $\delta t = 1$ (13%), $0.393$ against $0.500$ at $\delta t = 2$ (27%), where they are visibly different curves. - The shortcut reaches 1 at $\delta t = 4$ and 2.5 by the right-hand edge of the plot, while the exact probability flattens towards 1, reaching $0.918$. - The product $\gamma\,\delta t$ is not a probability. It is the rate accumulated over the window, the cumulative hazard. With a constant rate the probability of *not* recovering is $e^{-\gamma\,\delta t}$, so the probability of recovering is its complement $1 - e^{-\gamma\,\delta t}$, which cannot leave $[0, 1]$. - In a discrete-time model this has consequences. Once $\gamma\,\delta t$ exceeds 1, using it as a transition probability can remove more people from a compartment than it holds and push it below zero. The exact conversion stays inside $[0, 1]$ at any step width, and a small enough step keeps the shortcut close to it. The discrete-time session returns to this. ### Part C — random numbers you can reproduce ::: {#cell-ws-p01-c1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} λ0 = p.β * p.c * u0[2] / p.N # force of infection at the start p_infect = rate_to_proportion(λ0, 1.0) # An RNG produces a stream of numbers. Recreating it with the same # seed restarts that stream from the beginning. rng_demo = StableRNG(2024) first_five = rand(rng_demo, 5) next_five = rand(rng_demo, 5) first_five_again = rand(StableRNG(2024), 5) check("the same seed replays the same stream", first_five == first_five_again) check("drawing from an RNG advances its stream", first_five != next_five) function infected_today(rng, n_susceptible, p_infect) draws = rand(rng, n_susceptible) return count(draws .< p_infect) end today = infected_today(StableRNG(1), 990, p_infect) println("of 990 susceptibles, ", today, " are infected today") # One million independent trials, to check that their long-run # frequency approaches p_infect. fraction = infected_today(StableRNG(2), 1_000_000, p_infect) / 1_000_000 check("the observed fraction matches the probability", isapprox(fraction, p_infect; rtol = 0.05)) (; p_infect, fraction, today) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ the same seed replays the same stream ✓ drawing from an RNG advances its stream of 990 susceptibles, 3 are infected today ✓ the observed fraction matches the probability ``` ::: ::: {#ws-p01-c1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (p_infect = 0.004987520807317687, fraction = 0.004967, today = 3) ``` ::: ::: #### C1. Interpret - With $\lambda = 0.005$ per day a given susceptible is infected today with probability $1 - e^{-0.005} = 0.004988$, so the expected count across 990 susceptibles is about 4.9. `StableRNG(1)` happens to give 3. - Seeds 1 to 12 give 3, 3, 7, 8, 7, 6, 0, 3, 5, 3, 5, 5 — from none at all to more than one and a half times the mean. The spread is roughly the square root of the mean, so at these counts the day-to-day variation is comparable to the signal. - A day with no new infections is uncommon but not startling: it happens with probability $(1 - p)^{990} \approx 0.007$, about one day in 140. Seed 7 landing on it in a sample of twelve is luck. - The million-draw check recovers the probability to within half a percent, so the machinery is right and the variation is real randomness rather than a bug. **Against the deterministic answer** - Part A's corresponding quantity is the flow *into* $I$, $\lambda S = 4.95$ per day. That is `du[1]` with its sign flipped, not `du[2] = 2.45`, which is the *net* change in $I$ after recoveries. - The simulation's mean is $990 \times 0.004988 = 4.938$. The two agree to first order because $1 - e^{-x} \approx x$ for small $x$, and they would separate as the hazard or the window grew. - Neither average says how far a single realisation strays from it. With counts this small an outbreak started from a handful of cases can die out entirely, which no deterministic model started from the same state will predict. The jump-process session makes this concrete. **Local versus default generators** - The generator `rand` reaches for when none is named is shared state for the running task. Every draw anywhere advances it, so a result depends on how much random work happened *before* the function ran: a line added elsewhere, or two cells reordered, changes the numbers. - Passing an explicit `rng` makes that dependence visible and controllable. It does not make the function repeat itself: an RNG is mutable and drawing from it moves it along, which is why `next_five` differs from `first_five` even though both came out of the seeded `rng_demo`. - Only a freshly seeded generator replays the stream, so the cells above build a new `StableRNG(1)` and `StableRNG(2)` at each call site rather than reusing one. - `StableRNGs` adds the last piece: its stream is fixed across Julia versions and platforms, whereas the built-in generator may legitimately change between releases. ## Foundations: SIR theory and the Julia workflow — Day 1, Session 2 Worksheet: `worksheets/02-foundations-sir-theory-and-the-julia-workflow.qmd`. The chapter is [Foundations](../chapters/01-foundations.qmd). ::: {#ws-ch01-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using OrdinaryDiffEq using NonlinearSolve using CairoMakie check(name, condition) = println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint") function sir_ode!(du, u, p, t) S, I, R = u λ = p.β * p.c * I / p.N du[1] = -λ * S du[2] = λ * S - p.γ * I du[3] = p.γ * I return nothing end u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0] # S(0), I(0), R(0) p = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0) tspan = (0.0, 80.0) println("kernel ready; R₀ = ", p.β * p.c / p.γ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` kernel ready; R₀ = 2.0 ``` ::: ::: ### Part A — solve it, then read the answer ::: {#cell-ws-ch01-a1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} prob = ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p) sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5) check("the solver ran", sol.retcode == ReturnCode.Success) check("it stored one state every half day", length(sol.t) == 161) sol.u[end] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ the solver ran ✓ it stored one state every half day ``` ::: ::: {#ws-ch01-a1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3-element Vector{Float64}: 199.8228587945497 0.03697185303398417 800.1401693524167 ``` ::: ::: The kernel goes in by name: `sir_ode!`, not `sir_ode!(...)`. The solver calls it thousands of times with its own arguments, so what it needs is the function itself. ::: {#ws-ch01-a2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} t = sol.t S = sol[1, :] I = sol[2, :] R = sol[3, :] check("one value of I per stored time", length(I) == length(t)) check("the epidemic took off", maximum(I) > u0[2]) check("nobody is created or destroyed", all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), p.N; atol = 1e-6), sol.u)) println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(I), digits = 1), " on day ", round(t[argmax(I)], digits = 1)) println("largest conservation error: ", maximum(abs(sum(u) - p.N) for u in sol.u)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ one value of I per stored time ✓ the epidemic took off ✓ nobody is created or destroyed peak infectious: 158.5 on day 17.5 largest conservation error: 4.547473508864641e-13 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ws-ch01-sir .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (720, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "number of individuals") lines!(ax, t, S; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "S") lines!(ax, t, I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "I") lines!(ax, t, R; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 3, label = "R") axislegend(ax; position = :rc) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ws-ch01-sir .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Baseline SIR epidemic: susceptible, infectious and recovered over 80 days. ::: ::: #### A1. Interpret - `lines!` needs a plain list of numbers, one per time, which is what `sol[2, :]` gives. `sol.u` is a vector of 161 *state vectors*, so its first element is `[990.0, 10.0, 0.0]`, not a number. Both hold the same data: `sol.u` slices it by time, `sol[i, :]` by compartment. - The conservation error is arithmetic, not modelling. `Tsit5` combines several derivative evaluations per step with floating-point weights, and the rounding does not cancel, so $S + I + R$ drifts from $N$ by order $10^{-13}$ people over 80 days — a few parts in $10^{16}$ of $N$, the floor set by double precision. - The cell prints the largest drift rather than quoting a figure, because the exact value moves with the solver, its tolerances and the package versions. - The check's $10^{-6}$ tolerance is six orders of magnitude looser than that floor: it is there to catch a mistyped equation, not to measure the solver. Tightening `reltol`/`abstol` shrinks the discretisation error but not the rounding floor. - Conservation holds because it is a property of the equations, not something the code enforces. The three right-hand sides sum to zero by construction, since every flow leaves one compartment and enters another, and a quantity with zero derivative does not change. A typo in `du[2]` almost always breaks it. ### Part B — the threshold, and when nothing happens ::: {#cell-ws-ch01-b1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} R₀ = p.β * p.c / p.γ peak_index = argmax(I) S_over_N_at_peak = S[peak_index] / p.N check("R₀ is 2 for the baseline", isapprox(R₀, 2.0; atol = 1e-9)) check("the peak sits on the threshold", isapprox(S_over_N_at_peak, 1 / R₀; rtol = 0.01)) # 1% relative (R₀ = R₀, threshold = 1 / R₀, S_over_N_at_peak = S_over_N_at_peak) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ R₀ is 2 for the baseline ✓ the peak sits on the threshold ``` ::: ::: {#ws-ch01-b1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (R₀ = 2.0, threshold = 0.5, S_over_N_at_peak = 0.5005887830839842) ``` ::: ::: - The susceptible fraction at the peak lands on $0.5 = 1/R_0$ within tolerance. It is inexact only because the solution was stored every half day, so `argmax` finds the largest *stored* value; the ordinary differential equations session locates the peak exactly with a callback. - The equality describes a run that grows before it turns over, here $R_0 S(0)/N = 1.98$. The $c = 4$ run below has no such crossing: $I$ falls from day zero, its largest stored value is $I(0)$, and $S/N$ there is $0.99$. ::: {#cell-ws-ch01-b2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} contact_rates = [4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0] results = map(contact_rates) do c_val p_c = merge(p, (c = c_val,)) s = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p_c), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5) (c = c_val, R₀ = round(p_c.β * p_c.c / p_c.γ; digits = 2), peak_I = round(maximum(s[2, :]); digits = 1), infected_by_80 = round(1 - s[1, end] / p_c.N; digits = 3)) # no longer susceptible end check("each run used its own contact rate", length(unique(r.R₀ for r in results)) == 4) check("c = 4 gives R₀ below 1", results[1].R₀ < 1) check("prevalence does not grow at c = 4", results[1].peak_I <= u0[2]) check("the day-80 total climbs with contact rate", let a = [r.infected_by_80 for r in results]; issorted(a) && allunique(a) end) results ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ each run used its own contact rate ✓ c = 4 gives R₀ below 1 ✓ prevalence does not grow at c = 4 ✓ the day-80 total climbs with contact rate ``` ::: ::: {#ws-ch01-b2 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{c::Float64, R₀::Float64, peak_I::Float64, infected_by_80::Float64}}: (c = 4.0, R₀ = 0.8, peak_I = 10.0, infected_by_80 = 0.045) (c = 6.0, R₀ = 1.2, peak_I = 23.1, infected_by_80 = 0.327) (c = 8.0, R₀ = 1.6, peak_I = 87.5, infected_by_80 = 0.649) (c = 10.0, R₀ = 2.0, peak_I = 158.5, infected_by_80 = 0.8) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-ws-ch01-threshold .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig2 = Figure(size = (720, 400)) ax2 = Axis(fig2[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)", title = "Contact rate and the epidemic threshold") for c_val in contact_rates s = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, merge(p, (c = c_val,))), Tsit5(); saveat = 0.5) lines!(ax2, s.t, s[2, :]; linewidth = 3, label = "c = $(Int(c_val))") end axislegend(ax2; position = :rt) fig2 ``` ::: {#fig-ws-ch01-threshold .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Infectious curves across contact rates. Below c ≈ 5.05 the initial infections fade without an epidemic: with 99% susceptible at the start, growth needs R₀S(0)/N > 1, which is a little more than R₀ > 1. ::: ::: #### B1. Interpret - At $c = 4$ the ten initial infectious people do infect others before they recover, so the attack rate is not zero. What is missing is *growth*: each infection produces fewer than one further infection, so each generation is smaller and the chain dies out. "No epidemic" means no self-sustaining transmission, not no transmission — and early case counts look similar either way, so what separates them is the trend, not the level. - $R_0 = 1$ at $c = 5$, but that is the threshold for a *fully* susceptible population. With 1% already infectious, prevalence grows only when $R_0 S(0)/N > 1$, needing $c > \gamma/(\beta s_0) \approx 5.05$ where $s_0 = 0.99$. At $c = 5$ the product is $0.99$ and $I$ declines from day zero. - The threshold depends on how many remain susceptible, not on how many are currently infectious. So a falling case count and a controlled epidemic are different claims: a fall caused by using up susceptibles holds as long as $S/N$ stays below the $1/R_0$ that returns when control ends, while a fall bought by control can reverse, because the susceptibles it protected are still there. Case counts alone do not separate the two. - The steepest gains are near $R_0 = 1$. Between $c = 4$ and $c = 6$ the day-80 total moves from 4.5% to 32.7%; the same step from $c = 8$ to $c = 10$ moves it from 65% to 80%, and adding $c = 20$ reaches 98%, so doubling transmission from the baseline buys only 18 more points. - Final size is not the whole story. Over that same $c = 8$ to $c = 10$ range the *peak* goes from 88 to 158, and the peak is what determines whether hospitals cope. Cutting $c$ from 10 to 8 leaves $R_0$ at 1.6, well above 1, yet spares about 15% of the population an infection while nearly halving the peak. An intervention too weak to reach the threshold still changes the picture, and a decision usually rests on both numbers. ::: {.callout-note} The column is `infected_by_80`, computed as $1 - S(80)/N$, rather than `attack_rate`, and the distinction is not cosmetic. - It counts everyone no longer susceptible at day 80, whether recovered or still infectious. $R(80)/N$ would miss the ones still infectious, which matters exactly when the epidemic has not finished. - At $c = 6$ the three numbers separate: $R(80)/N = 0.321$, infected by day 80 is $0.327$, and the eventual attack rate is $0.348$. At $c = 10$ the epidemic is over by day 80 and all three agree to three figures. - Part C computes the final size directly, without simulating. ::: ### Part C — the final size, without simulating ::: {#cell-ws-ch01-c1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} s₀ = u0[1] / p.N residual(s, R0) = s - s₀ * exp(-R0 * (1 - s)) fs_prob = NonlinearProblem(residual, 0.2, R₀) s_inf = solve(fs_prob, NewtonRaphson()).u attack_rate = 1 - s_inf check("s∞ is a fraction, smaller than s₀", 0 < s_inf < s₀) check("it really is a root", isapprox(residual(s_inf, R₀), 0.0; atol = 1e-8)) sol_long = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, (0.0, 400.0), p), Tsit5(); reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10, save_everystep = false) simulated = sol_long.u[end][1] / p.N check("analytic and simulated agree", isapprox(s_inf, simulated; atol = 1e-3)) (s_infinity = round(s_inf; digits = 4), simulated = round(simulated; digits = 4), attack_rate = round(attack_rate; digits = 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ s∞ is a fraction, smaller than s₀ ✓ it really is a root ✓ analytic and simulated agree ``` ::: ::: {#ws-ch01-c1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (s_infinity = 0.1998, simulated = 0.1998, attack_rate = 0.8002) ``` ::: ::: The starting guess is not a free choice: the equation has a second root above 1, and a large guess such as $0.9$ converges to that one. ::: {#ws-ch01-c2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} turning_point = 1 - log(s₀ * R₀) / R₀ for guess in (0.2, 0.65, turning_point, 0.9) s = solve(NonlinearProblem(residual, guess, R₀), NewtonRaphson()) println("guess ", rpad(round(guess; digits = 4), 8), " value ", rpad(round(s.u; digits = 6), 10), " residual ", rpad(round(residual(s.u, R₀); digits = 6), 10), " ", s.retcode) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` guess 0.2 value 0.199796 residual -0.0 Success guess 0.65 value 0.199796 residual -0.0 Success guess 0.6585 value 0.658452 residual 0.158452 Unstable guess 0.9 value 1.010001 residual 0.0 Success ``` ::: ::: - The residual turns over at $s = 1 - \ln(s_0 R_0)/R_0 \approx 0.658$, which is what puts two roots there. That explains why there are two roots, not which guess ends at which one. - Starting exactly on the turning point shows the difference: the slope is zero, Newton's first step is undefined, and the solve fails instead of reaching either root — the value returned is the guess itself, with a residual of $0.16$. - The value and the residual are what identify a root. The return code is a useful signal alongside them, though which code a failure produces can change between package versions, which makes it a weak thing to build a check around. - Both converged values solve the equation, but only one can be a susceptible fraction: $s_\infty = 1.010$ would mean more people finished susceptible than started. That is why the worksheet checks $0 < s_\infty < s_0$, a stronger test than `retcode = Success`, which the root above 1 earns too. Deciding which root is the epidemic is the modeller's job, not the solver's. #### C1. Interpret - The epidemic ran out of *infectious people*, not susceptible ones. Once enough of the population sits in $R$, the susceptible fraction drops below $1/R_0$ and every infection produces less than one replacement, so prevalence falls even though 20% could still in principle be infected. - It overshoots first — transmission does not stop the instant $S/N$ crosses $1/R_0$, because a large infectious pool is still working through — and then stops well before everyone is reached. The remaining susceptibles are protected by the immunity around them, not by anything about themselves. - The final-size relation collapses $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ into $R_0 = \beta c/\gamma$, so any parameter set with the same $R_0$ gives the same total. What it discards is *time*. - Doubling $\beta c$ and $\gamma$ together leaves $R_0$ and the initial state alone, so the epidemic traces the same path through $(S, I, R)$ and reaches the same peak of 158, but on day 8.8 instead of day 17.5. The wave is narrower, not taller: rescaling the rates rescales the clock. - A wave half as long is a different problem for a health service than one twice as long with the same crest, and the final-size relation is silent about both. It answers "how many, in the end", not "how fast, and how bad at once", which is usually the operational question. ## Ordinary differential equations — Day 1, Session 3 Worksheet: `worksheets/03-solving-odes-with-events.qmd`. The chapter is [Ordinary differential equations](../chapters/03-ordinary-differential-equations.qmd). ::: {#ws-ch03-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using OrdinaryDiffEq using DiffEqCallbacks using CairoMakie check(name, condition) = println(condition ? Interpret - Day 5 is much the best: about 414 people ever infected, against about 708 for day 20 and about 796 for day 40 — the last barely better than the 800 with no campaign at all. - The same 30% coverage protects a different number each time, because it is 30% *of whoever is still susceptible*. That is why acting early buys more than the difference in doses delivered would suggest. ### Part C — a lockdown that triggers itself ::: {#ws-ch03-c1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} capacity = 100.0 trigger_day = Float64[] capacity_condition(u, t, integrator) = u[2] - capacity function impose_restrictions!(integrator) integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = 0.02,)) # β drops push!(trigger_day, integrator.t) end # the third argument, `nothing`, means "fire on the way up only" cap_cb = ContinuousCallback(capacity_condition, impose_restrictions!, nothing) sol_cap = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5(); callback = cap_cb, reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8) check("the trigger fired", !isempty(trigger_day)) check("restrictions kept I near capacity", maximum(sol_cap(t)[2] for t in tt) < 1.1 * capacity) isempty(trigger_day) || println("restrictions imposed on day ", round(trigger_day[1], digits = 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ the trigger fired ✓ restrictions kept I near capacity restrictions imposed on day 11.0 ``` ::: ::: #### C1. Interpret - The trigger fires on day 11.0 and the infectious curve tops out at almost exactly the capacity of 100. - The scheduled campaign in Part A requires knowing *when* to act, and so requires knowing in advance how the epidemic will unfold. The triggered lockdown watches instead, and needs a reliable, timely measurement of $I(t)$ — in practice the harder requirement, since surveillance reports cases late and incompletely. The observation-model session makes that gap explicit. - The largest value of $I$ sits exactly at the trigger, not at a smooth top. Restrictions cut $\beta$ to $0.02$, which at $S = 782$ gives $\beta c S / N = 0.156$ against $\gamma = 0.25$, so $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t$ jumps straight from positive to about $-9.4$. - $I$ stays continuous but its slope does not, so the curve turns a corner rather than arching over, and root-finding on $\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t = 0$ would find nothing. Whenever a parameter switches mid-run, the switching times matter as much as the callback's own events. - Lifting the restrictions with `affect_neg!`, the third positional argument, does not work at this threshold. Imposing restrictions turns $I$ downward *at the same value of $I = 100$ that triggered them*, so the release condition is met at the root the solver has just handled; it does not re-detect an event it has just processed, and the restrictions never come off. The run above shows one event at day 11 and no release for the remaining 69 days. The fix is **hysteresis**: two thresholds, plus a record of whether restrictions are currently active. It imposes at $I = 100$, releases lower at $I = 60$, and lets the condition watch whichever threshold currently applies. ::: {#cell-ws-ch03-c2 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} restrictions_on = Ref(false) policy_log = Tuple{Float64,Symbol}[] # watch 100 while free, 60 while locked down hysteresis_condition(u, t, integrator) = restrictions_on[] ? u[2] - 60.0 : u[2] - 100.0 function toggle_restrictions!(integrator) restrictions_on[] = !restrictions_on[] integrator.p = merge(integrator.p, (β = restrictions_on[] ? 0.02 : 0.05,)) push!(policy_log, (integrator.t, restrictions_on[] ? :impose : :release)) end sol_hyst = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode!, u0, tspan, p), Tsit5(); callback = ContinuousCallback(hysteresis_condition, toggle_restrictions!), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8) check("restrictions were imposed and then lifted", length(policy_log) == 2) check("I never exceeded capacity", maximum(sol_hyst(t)[2] for t in tt) < 1.01 * capacity) [(round(t; digits = 2), what) for (t, what) in policy_log] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ restrictions were imposed and then lifted ✓ I never exceeded capacity ``` ::: ::: {#ws-ch03-c2 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2-element Vector{Tuple{Float64, Symbol}}: (11.0, :impose) (16.1, :release) ``` ::: ::: - Restrictions go on at day 11.0 and come off at day 16.1, once prevalence has fallen to 60. - The gap between the two thresholds is what stops the policy switching on and off repeatedly at a single value, and the `Ref` is what lets the condition remember which phase it is in. - The epidemic does not return to 100 after release: by day 16 enough susceptibles have been infected that it cannot regrow that far. ## Discrete-time models — Day 1, Session 4 Worksheet: `worksheets/04-discrete-time-models.qmd`. "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint") rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt) function sir_map_step(state, p, δt) S, I, R = state infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S recovery = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I return (S - infection, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery) end function iterate_model(step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; extra = ()) traj = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1) traj[:, 1] .= u0 state = Tuple(float.(u0)) for k in 1:nsteps state = step(state, p, δt, extra...) traj[:, k + 1] .= state end return traj end u0 = [990, 10, 0] p = (β = 0.05, c = 10.0, γ = 0.25, N = 1000.0, ω = 0.02) δt = 1.0 nsteps = 728 # two years, and exactly 104 whole weeks ts = 0:nsteps sir_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sir_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps) println("R₀ = ", p.β * p.c / p.γ) println("peak infectious: ", round(maximum(sir_traj[2, :]), digits = 1)) println("infectious at two years: ", round(sir_traj[2, end], digits = 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R₀ = 2.0 peak infectious: 200.9 infectious at two years: 0.0 ``` ::: ::: ### Part A — immunity that does not last The third transition needs one new line and two changed terms. `waning` is a number of people, exactly like `infection` and `recovery`: the conversion turns the rate `p.ω` into a per-step proportion, and multiplying by `R` turns that proportion into a count. ::: {#cell-ws-ch02-a1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sirs_map_step(state, p, δt) S, I, R = state infection = rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt) * S recovery = rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt) * I waning = rate_to_proportion(p.ω, δt) * R return (S - infection + waning, I + infection - recovery, R + recovery - waning) end sirs_traj = iterate_model((s, p, dt) -> sirs_map_step(s, p, dt), u0, p, δt, nsteps) # What the continuous-time theory predicts for the endemic state. R₀ = p.β * p.c / p.γ S_endemic = p.N / R₀ I_endemic = p.N * (1 - 1 / R₀) / (1 + p.γ / p.ω) check("population still conserved", all(k -> isapprox(sum(sirs_traj[:, k]), p.N; atol = 1e-8), 1:nsteps+1)) check("immunity is waning", sirs_traj[1, end] > 300) check("the disease is still circulating after two years", sirs_traj[2, end] > 10) check("the model has settled down", abs(sirs_traj[2, end] - sirs_traj[2, end-28]) < 0.01 * sirs_traj[2, end]) check("prevalence lands within 30% of the analytic endemic level", isapprox(sirs_traj[2, end], I_endemic; rtol = 0.3)) (; S_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[1, end]; digits = 1), I_at_two_years = round(sirs_traj[2, end]; digits = 1), S_endemic = round(S_endemic; digits = 1), I_endemic = round(I_endemic; digits = 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ✓ population still conserved ✓ immunity is waning ✓ the disease is still circulating after two years ✓ the model has settled down ✓ prevalence lands within 30% of the analytic endemic level ``` ::: ::: {#ws-ch02-a1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (S_at_two_years = 447.4, I_at_two_years = 45.4, S_endemic = 500.0, I_endemic = 37.0) ``` ::: ::: The endemic values come from setting all three continuous flows to zero: $$ \frac{S^\ast}{N} = \frac{1}{R_0}, \qquad I^\ast = N\,\frac{1 - 1/R_0}{1 + \gamma/\omega}, $$ which for the baseline with $\omega = 0.02$ gives $S^\ast = 500$ and $I^\ast \approx 37$. The dotted line is the endemic level predicted by continuous-time theory. ::: ::: #### A1. Interpret - With waning the first wave peaks at 209 on day 19, against 201 on day 18 without it. Prevalence then falls to a trough of 19.3 on day 60, rises to a smaller second wave of about 61 around day 107, and settles at 45 infectious with 447 susceptible. - The early epidemic is almost unchanged because the waning flow is $\omega R_t$ and $R_t$ starts at zero: for the first fortnight there is nobody to lose immunity, and the two curves stay within 1% of each other through day 13. - What ends that is the size of $R_t$, not the passage of time. Once the wave has built a recovered pool, the gap opens fast — 5% by day 20, 10% by day 24 — enough to lift the peak from 201 to 209 and push it a day later. "No difference early" is an approximation, and $R_t$ is what marks when it stops holding. - The trough refills with susceptibles. The wave ends because $S$ fell below $N/R_0$, not because the pathogen went anywhere, and immunity keeps expiring at rate $\omega R$ while prevalence is low. Once $S$ climbs back above the threshold transmission grows again, giving the second wave and a damped oscillation towards the endemic level rather than a smooth approach. - The plateau sits above the analytic line because of the step size. Both flows use $1 - e^{-r\delta t}$, which understates $r\delta t$ more when $r\delta t$ is larger: recovery has $\gamma\delta t = 0.25$ and is throttled by 11.5% (0.2212 instead of 0.25), while infection has $\beta c I \delta t / N \approx 0.023$ and is throttled by only 1.1%. - Per step the map therefore recovers people relatively more slowly than it infects them, so the balance point moves to fewer susceptibles and more infectious. This is a property of $\delta t = 1$ day, not of the model: the step is a quarter of the 4-day infectious period, while the 50-day immunity is finely resolved by comparison. #### A2. That is probably smaller than the uncertainty in $\omega$, since "immunity lasts 50 days" is a guess to within a factor of two — but the two are not equivalent. Parameter uncertainty is a fact about the world; this bias is a choice, it costs nothing to remove, and nothing in the output announces it. - It grows quickly. A weekly step, $\delta t = 7$, tempting when the data are weekly, lands on $(S, I) = (279, 98)$, nowhere near the continuous-time model it is meant to approximate. - The step width is a numerical decision rather than a reporting one. Weekly data is a reason to aggregate a finely-stepped model up to weeks, as in Part C, rather than to step it weekly. ### Part B — the same model with integer people ::: {#cell-ws-ch02-b1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sirs_chain_step(state, p, δt, rng) S, I, R = state Y = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, S), rate_to_proportion(p.β * p.c * I / p.N, δt))) Z = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, I), rate_to_proportion(p.γ, δt))) W = rand(rng, Binomial(round(Int, R), rate_to_proportion(p.ω, δt))) return (S - Y + W, I + Y - Z, R + Z - W) end nsims = 100 chain_ens = [iterate_model(sirs_chain_step, u0, p, δt, nsteps; Runs that reach zero infectious stay there. ::: ::: #### B1. Interpret - Eight of the 100 realisations died out, seven between days 57 and 101 and one straggler on day 685. - That window is the trough. The first wave overshoots, driving $S$ well below the threshold, so prevalence collapses to a handful of cases — around 19 in the map and lower in many realisations. With that few, a short run of chance recoveries and no new infections wipes the disease out, and nothing brings it back. By the time waning has lifted prevalence to 40-odd cases, extinction needs a far longer unlucky streak. - The mean does not describe a typical realisation. At two years it is 40.9 against the map's 45.4, and most of that gap is the eight dead runs averaged in as zeros: the survivors average 44.5, within 2% of the map. - Even setting extinctions aside, there is no reason the survivors should land on the map. The map is the chain's expectation for *one step from a given state*, and the infection update is nonlinear, so iterating the map is a mean-field approximation of the ensemble mean, not the mean itself. - These 100 runs cannot show that. The survivors sit 0.9 below the map with a standard error of about 2, so a systematic gap is indistinguishable from sampling noise; 2000 runs would bring the standard error to 0.4 and resolve a gap of roughly one infectious person. What an ensemble can resolve sets the size of difference worth reading anything into. - The distribution is bimodal — faded out, or persisting near the endemic level — and the mean sits in a gap where no realisation lives, which is what averaging a bimodal outcome generally does. An absorbing state is the common way a model acquires one. - Only the chain can say whether the disease is still here in five years, and it answers a narrower question than the map appears to. The map moves fractions of people, so $I_t$ decays towards zero without arriving: extinction is a question its state space cannot represent, and its "endemic equilibrium" is permanent. - The chain has no permanent endemic state to offer in exchange. $I = 0$ is reachable from any state and nothing brings the disease back, so every realisation ends at zero if you wait long enough. Interpret - The integer initial condition is the only thing that changed between the two lowerings. Conservation holds exactly for a structural reason: each column of the stoichiometry matrix sums to zero, so every event moves one individual and creates none. The ODE conserves population only to solver tolerance. - The seeded trajectory peaks at 192 against the ODE's 158.45, and that is not evidence of the stochastic model being more explosive. One trajectory is not a mean, and the ensemble of 100 runs used in Part C peaks on average at 146.7, which sits *below* the ODE. - That ordering is the chapter's point about the discarded covariance. Interpret - The two objectives disagree, and not marginally: minimising $C(45)$ says start at $t_1 \approx 13.8$, minimising the peak says $t_1 \approx 9.6$. Retcodes tell you the solver finished cleanly, not that it finished anywhere useful. - The lesson is not "grid search everything", which does not scale past two or three decision variables. It is that a gradient method assumes a locally informative slope, and that assumption should be checked: sweep the objective in one dimension when you can, restart from several guesses when you cannot, and be suspicious of an optimizer that returns its own starting point. Writing `person.status` directly would let someone infected early in a sweep infect a later person in the same $\Delta t$, depending on an ordering with no meaning in the model, and the default `Schedulers.fastest` order is not even documented. Committing in `model_step!` makes every agent in a step read the same state. - The three runs peak at 76, 87 and 86 and end with 616, 766 and 652 recovered; the ODE peaks at 158.5 and ends at 800.2. The spread between runs is Monte Carlo variation, much of it in timing (peaks at $t = 17.6$, $41.6$ and $21.5$). The gap to the ODE is not: contacts are spent on neighbours who have already had the infection, and no number of replicates removes that. - With contacts from the whole population the ABM mean peaks at 156.8 against 158.5 and ends at 812.1 against 800.2, an RMSE of 8.4 people; from twenty-four neighbours the same numbers are 77.4, 688.4 and 28.9. Only the contact draw differs, so the rest of the code is exonerated and the gap is located in that one line. - A passing control does not show the contact draw is *right*. A wrong radius, a diamond metric, a grid that fails to wrap or a neighbour set holding the focal person would all pass it. `ws-ch06-c3c` covers that gap by testing the neighbourhood directly: uniform degree 24 and 8 pins radius, metric and wrapping, and self-exclusion and symmetry rule out two more faults. - This is the general move for a model with no analytic reference: find a limit that has one, check it, then restore the one ingredient under study and attribute what changes to it. At these settings the first wins, so the coarse step shows a net bias, not either effect alone. - $\Delta t$ is both: at every finite value it defines frozen-step semantics, a different process, and shrinking it is how you approach the process intended.
